lines.text: That pigeon isn't bobbing its head. Its head is standing still.
lines.see: Low side shot of a pigeon strutting on a night pavement, camera tracking the body so the head seems to bob

lines.text: Watch the head, not the body.
lines.see: The camera stops tracking and locks in space: the amber eye freezes in frame while the body slides forward under it

lines.text: The body walks forward underneath. The head stays locked in space.
lines.see: Ghost trail: amber head stamps pile up on one spot, grey body ghosts spread out along the pavement

lines.text: Then, snap. It jumps ahead and locks again.
lines.see: The head thrusts forward with an amber streak, a new stamp lands, crane up to show a row of stamps like footprints

lines.text: Here's the weird part. It's not for balance. It's for its eyes.
lines.see: Push in to the side of the head, the amber eye fills the frame

lines.text: While the head is frozen, the picture on its eye stays sharp.
lines.see: Through the eye: the pigeon's view on a curved retina, crisp while the head holds, smeared when it thrusts

lines.text: In 1978, a scientist put pigeons on a treadmill.
lines.see: Pull back out of the eye into a dark lab, a treadmill under a clear box, headline 1978 counts up

lines.text: Their world stopped sliding past. And the bobbing stopped too.
lines.see: The belt scrolls, the pigeon walks in place, its head stays dead still, ghost stamps sit on one point

lines.text: One pigeon, on a belt too slow to walk, held its head so still it fell over.
lines.see: Belt creeps, the body leans further and further forward under a fixed head until the pigeon tips over

lines.text: Its head is frozen about 63% of every walk.
lines.see: Crane up over a night plaza of walking pigeons, every head a still amber point, 63% counts up

lines.text: Chickens do it too. Now you can't unsee it. Genius, or just a silly walk?
lines.see: A hen struts past, then back to the same pigeon on the pavement (loop to frame 0), question headline, comment bubble

facts.claim: Head-bobbing whilst walking has two phases: one where the head is 'locked' in space but moves backward relative to the forward-moving body, and another where it is thrust rapidly forward to a new position

Head-bobbing is abolished when pigeons walk on a treadmill; if walking velocity matched belt velocity no head-bobbing movements were produced, suggesting it is primarily a visual response rather than one for balance (equilibratory)
Frost (1978): the head is stationary approximately 63% of the time during walking; forward head thrusts approximately 0.61 m/s

Frost (1978): when the treadmill was accidentally left on a very slow setting, too slow to induce walking, one bird's head was slowly pushed forward until it eventually toppled over; the slow belt was enough to make it stabilise its head even at the cost of balance
Head-bobbing occurs in at least 8 of the 27 orders of birds, including pigeons, doves, hens, starlings, pheasants, coots, quail and others (Frost 1978)
Troje & Frost (2000): one function of head-bobbing is to stabilise the retinal image during the hold phase; hold phase was 54% and 59% of the time in their two data sets
Head-bobbing is widely considered an optokinetic response that ensures retinal image stabilisation during the hold phase (Theunissen & Troje 2017)

publish.caption:
A walking pigeon's head is locked still in space about 63% of the time, while its body walks forward underneath. It's not for balance, it's to keep its view sharp. Put it on a treadmill and the bobbing stops.

Genius or silly walk? 👇
